title: SRE Standards: SLOs, Error Budgets, Capacity Planning, Reliability Initiatives, Incident Reviews, and Runbooks
author: Ari Chen
body:
Summary

This document defines Redwood Inference's SRE standards for Service Level Objectives (SLOs) and error budgets, capacity planning, reliability initiatives, incident review standards, operational tooling expectations, and runbook templates. It consolidates existing best practices, required metrics, ownership conventions, and procedural steps to ensure consistent reliability and predictable operational behavior across hosted, dedicated, and private deployments.

Goals

- Provide a single authoritative reference for SRE-related documentation.
- Standardize how SLOs are written, measured, and enforced.
- Ensure capacity planning is tied to traffic forecasts, error budgets, and business priorities.
- Define a repeatable incident review and reliability initiative workflow.
- Provide operational tooling and runbook templates that are actionable during on-call and postmortem work.

1) SLOs and Error Budgets

Intro and rationale

SLOs are the contract between product/engineering and users. Error budgets are the operational allowance for unreliability that lets teams balance feature velocity and stability. Every customer-facing service and internal critical system must have at least one SLO defined and a clear error budget policy.

SLO format (required)

Each SLO must be recorded in the SLO registry with the following fields:

- service_name (string)
- slo_name (string)
- objective (human-readable; e.g., "99.95% success rate over 30d")
- target (numeric) e.g., "99.95%"
- window (duration) e.g., "30d" or "90d"
- primary_metric (e.g., p99 latency, success_rate, availability)
- measurement_query (PromQL/SQL/metric path)
- owner (team/email)
- alerting_policy_id (link)
- error_budget_policy (string: automatic_rollout_block | manual_review | no_block)
- business_impact (short description)

Example SLOs

- api-generation-latency: objective=99.9% p99 <= 350ms, window=30d, primary_metric=p99_latency, owner=eng-serving-runtime
- control-plane-availability: objective=99.99% success_rate, window=90d, primary_metric=successful_requests/total_requests, owner=eng-platform

Calculations and conventions

- Availability/success_rate is defined as (successful requests / total valid requests), excluding known maintenance windows.
- Latency SLOs must use the p99 or p95 quantile as specified in the SLO. Do not average percentiles across hosts; use distribution-aggregation methods (trace through our observability-standard).
- Error budget burn rate = (observed_unavailability / allowed_unavailability) over the evaluation window.

Error budget policy and automated responses

- Green (burn_rate < 1): normal operations; changes and feature rollouts proceed as planned.
- Yellow (1 <= burn_rate < 5): restrict large-scale risky rollouts; require engineering review and runtime mitigations (canarying, reduced concurrency).
- Red (burn_rate >= 5): immediate rollback/mitigation of the primary cause; pause non-essential deployments for the affected service; schedule an incident review within 3 business days.

Ownership and communication

- Team owning SLOs is responsible for measurement accuracy, alerts, dashboards, and maintaining runbooks.
- The SRE org maintains the SLO registry and performs quarterly audits for coverage gaps.
- When an error budget policy triggers a Yellow or Red state, SRE on-call will notify the service owner and product stakeholders via the standard escalation channel (PagerDuty + #incidents).

2) Capacity planning

Principles

- Capacity planning ties expected user demand (traffic growth, campaign events) to resource allocation (GPU/VCPU, memory, throughput) with safety margins based on SLO criticality.
- Plan for graceful degradation: define lower-cost model variants and routing fallbacks that reduce cost when capacity pressure happens.

Required artifacts

- 12-month capacity forecast (monthly granularity)
- Quarterly scaling playbook (who to call, autoscale knobs, quota requests)
- Critical-path RTL (recovery time lines for capacity-related incidents)

Sizing methodology (summary)

1. Baseline: current 95th-percentile steady-state usage per region and per model.
2. Growth: apply product forecasts + historical seasonality.
3. Safety margin: +20% for high-priority services (SLO >= 99.9%), +40% for emerging workloads.
4. Burst capacity: maintain a pool sized for 3x typical per-request concurrency for 5-minute windows for customer-facing hosted API.

Capacity runbook template (table)

| Item | Description | Owner | Threshold | Action |
|---|---|---:|---|---|
| GPU pool usage | % used across cluster | eng-infra | > 75% 5m | Trigger autoscale; notify capacity-oncall |
| Queuing delay | average queue time | eng-serving-runtime | > 200ms p95 | Throttle lowest-priority routes; enable burst capacity |
| Model load failures | model load error rate | eng-serving-runtime | > 1% | Roll back last deployment; increase replicas |

Autoscaling and quotas

- Autoscaling rules must be codified in terraform and in the cloud autoscaler definitions.
- Dedicated customers have separate capacity commits; SRE and sales coordinate reserved capacity reviews quarterly.

3) Reliability initiatives (RIs)

Process

- When recurring incidents, error budget exhaustion, or capacity shortfalls are identified, open a Reliability Initiative (RI) ticket in the tracking board with: summary, impact, hypothesis, owners, due date, and success criteria (targeted SLI improvement or burn-rate reduction).
- RIs follow a standard lifecycle: Triage -> Plan -> Implement -> Measure -> Close.

Priority and resourcing

- High: immediate funding, cross-team engineering allocation (example: reduce model load time from 10s to 500ms).
- Medium: sprint-backed improvement (example: add additional prefilling for common model prefixes).
- Low: backlog item for continuous improvement.

Success metrics

- Quantifiable change in SLI (e.g., p99 latency improved 20%) or sustained reduction in error budget burn.

4) Incident review and postmortem standards

Scope

- All Sev >= 2 incidents must have a post-incident review within 7 calendar days. Sev 1 incidents require a blameless postmortem within 3 business days.

Postmortem structure (required sections)

1. Summary: one-paragraph impact and timeline.
2. Timeline: concise event timeline with timestamps.
3. Root cause analysis: explain technical root cause(s).
4. Contributing factors: human/process/automation gaps.
5. Remediation actions: short-term mitigations and long-term fixes with owners and due dates.
6. Follow-up: list Reliability Initiatives opened from the incident.
7. Lessons learned and monitoring changes.

Blameless language

- Use neutral, factual language; focus on system and process improvements, not individuals.

Incident review meeting cadence

- For Sev1/Sev2, schedule a 60-minute review with service owners, SRE on-call, and stakeholders. Record decisions and action owners in the ticketing system.

5) Operational tooling and observability expectations

Telemetry minimums

Every customer-facing service must expose the following metrics at 10s resolution:

- request_count (by route, model, region)
- request_success_count / request_failure_count (categorized by error class)
- latency_histogram (p50/p95/p99)
- queue_length / backpressure_signals
- model_load_time and model_memory_usage

Logging and traces

- Structured JSON logs containing request_id, route, model_id, upstream_id, user_id (hashed if PII), and error_code.
- Distributed tracing with sampling configuration tied to error budget state (increase sampling when burn_rate > 1).

Dashboards and alerts

- Each SLO must have a dashboard showing the SLI trend, burn rate, and recent incidents.
- Alert rules must map to playbook-runbook steps and include runbook links in the alert payload.

Tooling inventory (minimum)

- Metrics: Prometheus + Cortex (long-term)
- Traces: Jaeger/OpenTelemetry
- Logging: ELK or hosted equivalent
- Paging: PagerDuty
- Incidents & Postmortems: JIRA / Confluence templates

6) SRE runbooks (templates and examples)

Runbook conventions

- Runbooks must be concise, step-by-step, and tested at least once per quarter (runbook rehearsals).
- Each runbook page should include: symptom, primary checks, quick mitigations, escalation path, and full recovery procedure.

Runbook template (recommended)

- Title
- Service / component
- PagerDuty escalation policy link
- Symptoms (what the on-call will see)
- Initial checks (commands, dashboards, queries)
- Quick mitigations (commands/playbook to reduce impact)
- Full recovery steps (detailed rollback or configuration changes)
- Post-incident actions and ticket references

Example: API high-latency runbook (summary)

Symptoms

- P95 > 500ms or p99 > 1s, queue growth, and error rates slightly elevated.

Initial checks

1. Check service CPU/GPU utilization and queue_length: query Prometheus: "sum(rate(requests[1m])) by (instance)"
2. Confirm model load errors: check logs for "model_load_error" in the last 10m.

Quick mitigations

1. Enable degraded routing: switch traffic to lower-latency model variant (documented routing flag).
2. Reduce concurrency for non-critical routes via feature flag.

Full recovery

1. If mitigation solved the issue, open a Reliability Initiative to address root cause.
2. If not, roll back last configuration/deployment and scale up GPU pool as per capacity runbook.

Testing and rehearsal

- Runbooks must be exercised during quarterly game days. Evidence of rehearsal (notes and tickets) should be attached to the runbook page.

7) Governance and review cadence

- SLO and runbook audits: quarterly by SRE leads.
- Capacity review: monthly for high-priority services, quarterly for others.
- Postmortem review: within 7 days (Sev2) / 3 business days (Sev1).
- RI backlog: reviewed in the SRE weekly prioritization meeting.

Appendices

A: SLO checklist (quick)

- [ ] Defined objective and window
- [ ] Measurement query recorded
- [ ] Dashboard and alert created
- [ ] Error budget policy set
- [ ] Owner and reviewer assigned

B: Contact matrix (example)

- SRE on-call: pagerduty team "sre-oncall"
- Eng-serving-runtime: eng-runtime-oncall@redwood.example.com
- Product on-call: product-oncall@redwood.example.com

C: Useful queries (examples)

- Success rate: "sum(rate(successful_requests[30d])) / sum(rate(total_requests[30d]))"
- p99 latency: "histogram_quantile(0.99, sum(rate(request_duration_seconds_bucket[5m])) by (le))"
